processing: Okabe is best known for gyokuro, which as a class is shaded before picking, then steamed, rolled and dried. Sencha-style processing is the usual method for other Shizuoka greens.
harvest_season: As with other Japanese greens, the spring first flush is the prized picking; gyokuro is normally a first-flush tea.
appearance_dry: Typical of gyokuro: fine, dark green, needle-like leaves with a slight gloss.
appearance_liquor: Pale, clear yellow-green, as is usual for gyokuro.
appearance_wet: Soft, deep green leaves that open fully, typical of shaded tea.
taste_profile: Okabe gyokuro is described as mellow with a distinctive aroma; expect the savoury, brothy sweetness typical of shaded Japanese tea.

brewing.notes: Gyokuro guidance: cool water and a small pot bring out sweetness. Hot water pulls bitterness and loses the point of the shading.

vintage_note: Sold as a current-year spring tea, like other Japanese greens, and best drunk within about a year. Asahina gyokuro is often sold under the name of the individual grower.
description:
Okabe is a part of Fujieda in Shizuoka, and its tea is known above all for gyokuro from the Asahina district. It is placed alongside Uji and Yame as one of Japan's three great gyokuro areas, which is a surprise to anyone who thinks of Shizuoka only as sencha country.

Gyokuro is shaded before picking, which as a class keeps the leaf deep green and savoury and holds back astringency. In Asahina the tea is treated as a grower's craft: eight producers are known locally as gyokuro masters and their teas are sold under their own names.

Local descriptions stress a mellow flavour and a particular aroma. Brew it the way you would brew any gyokuro: plenty of leaf, little water, and far cooler water than instinct suggests. Most disappointing cups come from water that is too hot.

When buying, look for the Asahina name, the grower and the harvest year. Fujieda's roadside station Gyokuro no Sato has a tea room, Hyogetsu-tei, where you can taste it before buying.
history: Little is documented in accessible form about when gyokuro growing began in Asahina. What is clear is the present standing: Shizuoka Prefecture itself presents Okabe as a gyokuro area on a par with Uji and Yame, and the name is kept alive by named growers.
